rv.q: So in Fiddler on the Roof, a much-revived masterpiece whose greatness comes over sweet and strong in this bewitching revival by the director Jordan Fein, the light and the shade do the hora folk dance all evening.

And Julia Cheng’s reeling choreography is a riot –whether it’s toasting Tevye’s eldest daughter’s betrothal in the tavern (ominously interrupted by menacing Cossacks), or at the actual wedding, which has celebrants spinning like huge black spiders with bottles balanced on their heads.

Fein’s staging of the beloved Broadway musical loses that spine-tingling natural backdrop — a perfect match for the gradually darkening tale — but it fills the giant theatre with story, spirit, song and sorrow.
Jordan Fein’s staging remains joyful, exhilarating and humane, the big hits
It's a beautifully judged production of a classic: tradition tenderly rendered truly fresh.
Stripped of schmaltz and imbued with a genuine folk sensibility, this version of the story of Tevye the milkman and his neighbours in Anatevka is simply glorious.
It’s Fiddler with all the stuff you love about Fiddler
Jordan Fein’s superb Regent’s Park revival of Fiddler on the Roof has been transplanted to form the big summer musical offering at the Barbican.
This is a Fiddler that’s going to take us along at a gallop.
Julia Cheng’s choreography, just as electrifying as it was last year, is now given even more time in the spotlight, sitting centre-stage in a smaller space.

Julia Cheng’s exquisite dance sequences honour the musical’s Golden Age roots, as well as Jerome Robbins’s original choreography — specifically inclusion of the Bottle Dance, which delighted the audience on opening night.
Concentrating the cast into a tighter space focuses the energy and charges every dynamic with new electricity.
Now, as much as ever,Fiddler on the Roofis a historical lesson for today’s world.
Fein’s Fiddler on the Roof doesn’t just revisit a classic; it reclaims it with urgency and grace.

cn.t: Critics rave over Jordan Fein's Fiddler on the Roof at the Barbican — a powerful, emotionally resonant revival. Some mourn the lost magic of Regent's Park's open-air setting, but superb performances and electrifying choreography more than compensate.
